When I initially began writing this letter, I pulled four pages of excerpts from emails and text messages over the past two years in which I expressed feeling unheard, unsupported, and as though my boundaries were not being respected. After some thought, I deleted all of it.

Instead, I am going to ask you to pause here. Please go back and read the email I sent you on January 16th, 2026. Then, would you please reread our text message conversation from June 4th in its entirety.

I would like to point out that these conversations took place six months apart.

What I need to know is whether you can see the pattern I am describing. Not whether you agree with every detail, but whether you understand that this wasn't one argument for me. It was another repetition of something I have been trying to communicate for a long time.

It's about a long-standing pattern where my need for space during periods of stress has repeatedly been experienced as rejection, leading me to feel misunderstood, unsupported, and increasingly uncertain that my needs can be respected long-term.

Imagine feeling safe and secure in your relationship, and then something happens that cracks that sense of safety. The immediate hurt is one thing, but the real damage comes from realizing you've stood in this exact place before and remembering every previous fracture that never fully healed.

I imagine your interpretation of many of these events differs from mine because, more often than not, I eventually gave in. From your perspective, the issue may have been resolved. From mine, the issue was never resolved; I simply chose the path that created the least conflict. I meet the kids even though I am struggling under enormous pressure at work. I push myself beyond what I have to give while struggling with depression in order to meet your need for connection. I make the phone call even though I have repeatedly said I am not ready for it. More often than not, I leave those conversations feeling unheard, overwhelmed, and in tears.

If this happened once every few years, I could make peace with that.

However, if every year, one of us crosses a major boundary, the other person loses trust, we spend weeks recovering, and then we start over - that is not relationship work. It’s a recurring injury.

I don’t expect perfection from either one of us. I do expect growth. In other words, if this happens again, I don’t want us to simply be better at repairing it. I want us to be less likely to create it in the first place.

Every time something important comes up, I have to fight to have my needs taken seriously. I am exhausted from having to explain, re-explain, justify, and defend my need for space. I don’t want to spend years arguing the legitimacy of my needs. I no longer trust that asking for space will be respected when you are hurting.

As much as I want to be empathetic and understanding, your hurt does not entitle you to push past my boundaries. Your pain is real. Your need for connection is real. What has been painful for me is feeling as though my needs are repeatedly given less weight when they come into conflict with yours.

I appreciate the space you have provided me this week and the effort it has required. At the same time, part of what has been difficult is realizing that I have been asking for some version of this for a very long time. What has been difficult is realizing that receiving the space I asked for doesn't undo the loss of trust that came from feeling like I had to fight for it in the first place.

I suspect when I say “I don’t want to do another round of relationship work or emotional labor because I am exhausted”, you heard “I don’t want to work on the relationship”. What I actually mean is “I don’t have the emotional bandwidth to work on the relationship right now”.

Right now, I need a break from:

- Another relationship discussion
- Another explanation
- Another emotional demand
- Another attempt to solve something

There are a few questions I am wrestling with:

- Do you genuinely understand why this has affected me so deeply?
- Why did it have to get this bad before I was taken seriously?
- Is love enough when I don’t feel emotionally safe during conflict?
- Is this the kind of relationship dynamic I want to live with?
- If the conflict disappeared, if the pressure disappeared, if the uncertainty disappeared, would I still be excited about a future together?

The honest answer to all of these questions is ‘I don’t know’. I can't tell the difference between not wanting to do the work and being too exhausted to do the work.

The thought of doing relationship work right now fills me with dread, and I don't know whether that's because I'm burned out or because we have reached our end.

I know I want you. I am equally certain that I do not want the version of the relationship we have been living. Even though you have given me the space I needed this week, I am realizing that it may not be enough. I am looking at someone I love with my whole heart who is now making a genuine effort, but I’m still not finding myself pulled back towards the future we once imagined together.

I still love you, and I want to honestly see what I feel after some time and space. I do not want to make a permanent decision based on (hopefully) temporary emotions. The hope is that I will be able to start therapy with you in August refreshed and recharged.

I also recognize that it is not fair to ask you to wait around indefinitely while I figure out if I still want this relationship or not. I do not know how to address that. Only you can tell me what you can or cannot tolerate.

These are a lot of words to say that I don’t know a lot of things, but I wanted to try to give you an insight into where my thoughts are this week.

Today marks two years.

Two years since the day you died in front of me.

I could say it’s been two years since I lost you, but the truth is more complicated than that. Because a part of me got stuck in that moment. A part of me is still there, trying to understand how a life can end so suddenly.

I was your counselor.

I was supposed to help you through your darkest moments.

And yet, despite all my good intentions, despite everything I tried to do, I couldn’t stop the irreversible from happening.

Two years.

Two years spent trying to rebuild myself.

Two years reliving memories I never wanted to carry.

Two years wondering if I could have done more.

Two years carrying a weight I still don’t know what to do with.

Some wounds never truly heal. You just learn how to live with them.

And today, in the middle of Pride Month, I think about you even more.

I think about the person you were.

I think about the person you could have become.

And I think about everything that was denied to you.

Because you were trans.

And because I know how much other people’s judgment can hurt.

I came out as a trans person too, once.

I was afraid too.

Afraid of being rejected.

Afraid of losing the people I loved.

Afraid that people would never see me the same way again.

But I was incredibly lucky.

I had people around me who welcomed me with love.

People who listened.

People who supported me.

People who reminded me that I belonged here.

People who helped me keep moving forward when I didn’t think I could.

People who, without even knowing it, helped keep me alive.

And for the past two years, there has been one thought that never leaves me.

I wish you had that too.

I wish you had met people who truly saw you for who you were.

I wish someone had managed to convince you that you deserved to be loved exactly as you were.

I wish you had lived long enough to discover that there are people who stay. People who support. People who love without conditions.

Because nobody should have to go through this alone.

Because that’s what Pride Month is really about.

It’s not just flags, parades, or rainbow colors.

It’s stories.

It’s people who fought for the right to exist.

It’s people who were rejected by their families.

It’s young people lying awake at night wondering if anyone will ever love them for who they truly are.

It’s people who spent years hiding their identity because they were afraid.

Afraid of being abandoned.

Afraid of being mocked.

Afraid of being hated.

Afraid of losing everything they had.

Pride Month exists because for far too long, being different was treated as something that needed to be fixed instead of something worth celebrating.

It exists because too many LGBTQ+ people grew up believing they were alone.

Because too many people were told they were a burden.

Because too many people eventually came to believe they didn’t deserve a place in this world.

And even today, despite all the progress we’ve made, there are still young people living that reality.

Young people who are told they are the problem.

Young people who learn to hate themselves before they ever learn how to love themselves.

Young people who look toward their future with fear instead of hope.

So when I hear people say that Pride Month is no longer necessary, I think of you.

I think of your story.

I think of the pain you carried.

I think of everyone who is still carrying that same pain today.

And I tell myself that we cannot afford to stop talking about acceptance.

Because behind every statistic, there is a face.

Behind every number, there is a person who dreamed of a better life.

Behind every suicide, there is a story that deserved a different ending.

To me, Pride Month is not just a celebration.

It is a promise.

A promise to keep telling LGBTQ+ people that they belong here.

A promise to keep fighting so that no young person grows up believing they would be better off dead than alive.

A promise to build a world where being trans, gay, lesbian, bisexual, or non-binary is never a reason to suffer.

Because no identity should ever become a sentence.

Because no young person should have to die for being themselves.

Because no one should have to wait their entire life to hear the words, “I accept you exactly as you are.”

And because some absences remind us every day what happens when that acceptance never comes.

No one should have to carry the weight of rejection until they begin to believe that dying is the only way out.

People often talk about Pride Month as a celebration.

But for me, it is also a reminder.

A reminder that acceptance is not a bonus.

Acceptance saves lives.

Love saves lives.

Respect saves lives.

And the absence of those things can cost lives.

Two years later, I am still trying to move forward.

But there are days like today when everything feels like it’s falling apart.

Days when it feels like all the work I’ve done to heal disappears beneath the weight of a single memory.

Days when your absence hurts just as much as it did on the first day.

I don’t know if grief ever becomes easier with time.

I only know that I still carry your story with me.

And I know that if sharing this pain can help even one person feel seen, accepted, or loved today, then your memory will continue to give the very things you deserved so much in life: a little more understanding, a little more love, and a little more humanity.

You should have had more time.

You should have had more love.

You should have had the chance to discover that your life had immense value.

And even two years later, there are still days when I am shattered by your absence.

Because the truth is, I don’t just carry the memory of your death.

This year has just been a lot for me. I guess it started in 2023, May, when I was hospitalized for preeclampsia, my youngest son was born a 32w premie, and my son was diagnosed with brain cancer. That year was hard enough, but we pushed through. The hospital staff were very accommodating, putting both my sons under one hospital so I can be with them both. I am very blessed that we are all still alive. We went through all chemo rounds, traveling and we thought we would be done, but a year and a half later, my son’s cancer came back. From my son’s second cancer diagnosis, to my house flooding, to the whole gong show of going to the airport, to political struggles that could jeopardize my son’s treatment. During this journey, I’ve also bonded, made memories, and lost a lot of people this year. All of this year, they all just left, I will never get to see them anymore. Children and adults alike. Maybe I just feel overwhelmed with everything as I look back. 

There’s just this energy that’s dragging my heart down with every loss and I can’t explain this feeling to anyone. My husband expresses grief differently than I do, and it feels like nobody understands. Here I am looking for more internet strangers to validate my feelings. 

In the Ronald McDonald House (RMHC), it was really a city of misery. Everyone is miserable. Somehow, that was our common ground and many of us bonded this way. We became kinda like a family, exchanging our contact info, and supported each other. We had to use their services twice. Once in Calgary, and another time in Jacksonville. The Calgary RMHC, it was located very close to the hospice, so we knew what the end of our journey would look like if everything doesn’t go well. At the same time, all of us were dangling in that uncertainty. The main difference was that for many of us, it was our first treatment, so it was very hopeful, and easy to find good moments. 

When my son’s cancer came back, I was resentful. I cursed every child who was well because why not my son? Especially the parents who I got in touch with during the first diagnosis. All the times I encouraged them, and comforted them. Why my child and not theirs?

In the Jacksonville RMHC, many of us bonded over the fact that our first treatment had failed. Maybe even second or third. Some cannot even identify if they had cancer, but cysts just keep coming out of their brains. 

We listened to each other, we licked each other’s wounds, we went drinking together, we had outings with our kids. We were all very close to walking that plank of death with our children. What still haunts me was when a mom who had her child deceased for two years, but came back to support her sister, whose son was having seizures. She asked me what I would’ve done. Would I have continued to find clinical trials for that hope? Or just give up hope and spend the remaining days? Her daughter had the same brain tumour as Mattis. 

We all saw what that hell looked like. I knew I had lost the meaning to the word “hope” and I am still struggling to find what it actually means to me. I had criticism from different denominations of Christianity in these dark times because I didn’t have an answer. Yes, there were lots of parents in there also struggling, and there were some pastors who volunteer to listen, but they really didn’t need to criticize me. I hated the prospect of hope, always wanting more, like some gambling addiction of the best outcome no matter the odds. Hope is waiting, and I am tired. Especially when I didn’t understand what I was waiting for. 

It was a rude awakening when I heard that two of the children had passed the end of October (so two weeks from today as of writing this post). I’m scared. I’m really just sad. I don’t know if it’s projection, or grief, but just the memories of their laughter, their mischief, everything made me hurt. 

Then there are some regular customers who we’ve known for years. Some were my parents’ friends who saw us grow up. One in particular we loved their company. He always had a hot chocolate with a croissant. He was an artist, doing wood carvings, painting miniatures, doing all sorts of fascinating projects. He was diagnosed with dementia, and he just had an artery replacement. We thought he was doing better, but I guess when the time comes, it’s always unexpected. His passing also hit me hard. 

Now, like ebbs and flos of the tide, images, and memories of these people surface, and drags me down. I feel like drowning. 

This Sunday, I was at church for my niece’s first communion. They had a book of prayers for the faithful departed. As I was writing all the names this year, I’ve realized I’ve met many, bonded with many, made memories with many, and ultimately lost many. Nine total names, children and adults alike. I knew seven people well, and I put two other names of people who I cared about and they have lost their loved ones. 

I have this black ribbon tattoo on my back that I got for my birthday. I originally just wanted a standard ribbon as a remembrance of this whole hospital journey. Black ribbons mean grief and mourning. It’s almost like a calling, almost like me carrying grief on my back. It feels heavy. 

As I was writing, it felt like a mini funeral for me, like putting their names to rest. I just thought of the book, “A Fault in our Stars,” where I agree, funerals are for the living. 

I still have each of their names on my phone, as if cradling their memories with me, while also thinking about how I won’t see them for a long while. I still have their pictures, and it pains me to look through them. 

I thought I could lurk in these subreddits to find people with common ground, but it’s just become so overwhelming for me that it’s really hard for me to find comfort. Please help.

My grandma died 7 years ago due to heart failure, at least from what I can guess, and my aunts in particular still hold it against me.

Most of my memory about the events are blurry but I'll do my best to share.

Some background to this; in 2019 I was living with one of my aunts due to my mother having another episode where she had to stay at the local hospitals in-patient psychiatric ward for around 3-6 months, I don't remember exactly how long just that she went in after my birthday and was released home a month or so before I graduated.

At the time, my aunt was running my grandmother to appointments because of this and I had to stay with my grandma for one weekend during school holidays because my aunt was going to something.

The Monday my aunt was picking me up from my grandma's house, my grandma said she wasn't feeling well and that she didn't want to go to her appointment. I thought nothing of it and let her be and waited for my aunt to get there so we could go back to her place and I could do whatever it was I wanted to do at the time.

When my aunt got there she wondered why my grandma was still in bed, she explained she didn't feel well enough to go out and my aunt turned and asked me why I hadn't called or texted her about it. I just said I didn't think about it and she said that I should stop thinking about girl lifeguards and being on my phone, and focus more on communicating.

Mind you I mentioned if my cousin got any pictures of the female lifeguards while they were showing off pictures of the "hot" male lifeguards.

One scolding later, we get in her car and she drives the hour to her place. When we get there she gets a call from someone saying that we need to come back as something's happened to my grandma.

This is where the guilt and blame comes from, I remember I was just getting stuff unpacked thinking "man, it would be better if grandma just died". Immediately I felt guilty for even thinking that and was wondering where that thought even came from; I didn't share that with anyone at the time.

We get in the car and the whole drive all I can think about is why I thought that and how disgusted I was that my brain decided to want my grandma, who had been nothing but kind, dead.

The next part is a blur but I vaguely remember getting back to my grandma's house, my mother and her friend being there, the ambulance, my aunt telling me not to go inside, my mother trying to hug me as I scream at her to not touch me because I just wanted to cry on my own, then we're in a waiting room at the hospital, the rest of the family is there except one cousin who was out of state.

I don't remember how long we were in there but it must have been 4-6 hours, stuck in a small room just hoping for news. Meanwhile, my mother is going on and on: "she's going to be fine", "she'll be good to go", etc. And by that point I was just so over the faux positivity that I snapped and said "you don't know that, she could be dying and you're being cheerful".

This set my mother off and she had to be walked back to the psych ward instead of continuing to wait with everyone.

When the doctor finally came in he said that my grandma was not in good condition and that we had the choice to keep her on life support with no quality of life or say our final goodbyes.

My aunts chose to let her pass in peace than subject us and her to being miserable.

When it was my turn to say goodbye to her all I could think of was my earlier thought, how I wish she'd just die so I wouldn't have to continuously be pulled to every appointment, every emergency and have to go to a her house nearly every night. My goodbye turned into sobbing I'm sorry, I just wanted to apologise for the thought I had, for brushing off her calls, for not wanting to visit her everyday.

I think one of my aunts and eldest cousin was in the room with me at the time and they were confused on why I was apologising but I couldn't explain, I just shut down.

I don't remember if it was days or weeks after but I remember my aunts had tried to ask me about it and being able to voice why

At one point, before the funeral, I was in the car with my eldest cousin and she asked me why I was apologising to my grandma; she said that my aunts thought I'd done something terrible to my grandma and that she didn't think I had but I should clear things up. I didn't want to feel more ostracised from them so I told the truth, about how I had a single thought that my grandma should die so life would be easier for everyone. I felt so guilty admitting it, it felt like saying it out loud would suddenly turn me into my grandma's killer.

My cousin said that a thought can't kill a person and that I might have had the thought because, subconsciously, I knew my grandma was dying.

Her reassurance did help a bit but didn't fully get rid of the weight in my chest.

Eventually, my cousin shared the reason with my aunts and they didn't bring it up to me after that.

More recently I had another altercation with my aunts involving my grandma's sewing machine and my cousin, trying to be the family mediator, shared that my aunts still believe I caused my grandma's death or that I was to blame.

I was honestly shocked because it had been about 6 years since and I had mentally blocked out most of that year because so much happened.

I haven't spoken to them about it since but the fact they believe I had some part in her death, even minute, hurts so much.

I'm glad I separated myself from that family but the thought still haunts me.

I’m in therapy, but no diagnosis or medication has helped. Also seeing doctors, since nothing has helped yet, ruling out anything physiological.

Me: “Are we okay?”        
Him: “Yes.”        
Me: “Do you resent me for anything?”        
Him: “No, why would I?”        
Me: “Is there anything bothering you that we need to fix?”

Lying back on the lounger in the garden with my hat over my face, noticing the pin pricks of light shining through the holes in the hat, I can almost hear Trish’s voice call out through the trellis fence… “Kathryn?” But she’s not there. The trellis fence is a relatively new addition separating our gardens, only a couple of years old. Our fence blew down in a bad storm and we replaced it with trellis. The trellis brought us closer together in a way, as we were able to have so many chats though it. 

On sunny warm days like this one, she would usually be in her garden mowing her lawn or weeding and tidying or having a cigarette. We would say hello to each other in passing and sometimes we would have a chat through the trellis, or she would be returning the dog after she escaped to eat the cat food in her garden. We lived next door to each other in semi-detached cottages for seven years and our relationship was sometimes uneasy and awkward. Mostly we disagreed on the number of feral cats that either of us wanted around the place and while we never had any explicit face to face disagreements about it, I did contact a cat charity about it and I think she knew. She told me many times how she preferred animals to people and considered cats her kindred spirits, which was why she put food out for the feral cat community in the area. I was worried about the health of the cats and the incessant kittens that would turn up in our hedges with diseased looking eyes and seemingly absent cat mothers. Otherwise, we chatted with each other, although I always felt that she mistrusted me in some way and people in general, which also caused uneasiness at times. Despite this, we shared some very deep and consequential conversations in our gardens that I will always remember. Trish was a very small woman, always with beautifully styled silvery grey bob who kept herself very well and active. I always felt huge when talking to her as she was so short and slim and tidy. It was a bit of a shock when she told me she was ill as she had seemed to active and well. I remember she had told me about a time when she was a very young woman, finding out that she had cancerous tumours in her womb and begging the doctors to please try to save it so that she could have children. But she never could and told me they thought she would die, so she was lucky to have survived it. She went to be nursed by nuns and the way she spoke about that experience, it seemed that their treatment of her affected her just as much as her illness. I didn’t know much about her earlier life, but she mentioned that she had fostered children for years and it broke her heart in the end, so she gave it up. There was no husband or children so she lived here alone, with the odd friend to visit from time to time. I’m not sure what age she was when she died, possibly late 70’s if I had to guess. 

Sometimes when I’m coming home at night and don’t see her car there, it hits me that she’s gone again and I’m sad. Like today, when she would usually be in her garden, there would be a conversation of some kind. She would never have let it get overgrown like it is now if she could possibly help it. I wonder what she would make of it now, quite overgrown since she left in October. I’m sure she would love to see all the different bird species around recently. I wonder about the hedgehogs and badgers that she used to watch eating the food in her garden at night. The buzzard that she used to leave food for. The birds who used to eat from her bird seed tray. Do they still come to her garden? She told me excitedly once that she spotted a rat and a hedgehog eating food side by side in her garden one night as if they were the best of friends. She really did love and have a deep respect for the natural world and animals. 

When she was very ill and told me that she didn’t have long left to live, she said she thought about when I told her about my mother and how young she was when she died of cancer. She never followed that up with how she felt about it all, but I hope she felt less alone. When she was very near the end she didn’t want a fuss and didn’t want to go to hospice, just to be at home with her cats. Marcus went to see her and took our dog to visit, as she loved our dog. I didn’t go. Maybe I didn’t think she’d want the fuss or awkwardness of whatever our relationship was, or maybe I was scared or maybe I didn’t realise she was so close to death or want to think that I wouldn’t see her after that…but I didn’t go to see her and I should have gone, I think. It’s hard to say and hard to acknowledge. I regret it.

It’s strange when your next-door neighbour dies. You’re so used to their presence on the other side of the wall, shared house issues, chats, difficult conversations, noises and exchanging Christmas presents. When you tell people your neighbour died, “that’s sad” they’ll say, and they’ll be thinking it’s not like you were that close, I suppose. And maybe that’s true, but even so…

Today, sitting in the garden and looking through the trellis at her overgrown garden that she tended to so well, wondering what the chat would be on this beautiful sunny day, I suppose you could say - I miss Trish and whatever our relationship was.

Trish didn’t want a fuss and left instructions that there was to be no funeral, no goodbyes. As time has gone on I feel that despite being Trish’s wish, it’s not right to not acknowledge her existence in some way. So, maybe I’m writing this so she can be acknowledged in a small way, for the brief time that I knew her.

I broke up with my ex about 3 years ago. It was a whirlwind romance fairlytale stuff. She was truthfully my first love. I could go on about the good times. But near the end cracks began to form. Combination of being young, too immature, lack of communication, and just not being where we want to in life. But we still loved each other. So much that we spent the better part of that first year apart still talking (which in hindsight was a mistake). She’d call and show me her outfits. But there was so much unresolved. Sometimes little comments would strike an old nerve and conversations would become screaming matches.

We knew we were talking to other people. I had an on and off "situationship" that became deeper and I felt guilty for enjoying my time with her. I can admit I was looking for a physical (and at times emotional) connection I wasn’t able to get from my ex. Fucked up but eventually that fell off because I felt I was betraying myself and my ex by not being all in on making things work.

Me and my ex went on some dates as I tried to reconnect and prove that I still cared about. We’d talk about the real things but it felt like when I wanted to give her a chance she would pull away and vice versa. Eventually we mutually decided some space was healthy.

Beginning of last year I asked her if we could really try and she told me that it's time to move on. Point blank period. Completely shut out. Shattered me. I was in a deep hole for a while. Blocked her on everything because it hurt too much to see her. I was reading into every song lyric, IG story, TikTok like/repost. I spent the better part of that year trying to come to terms with that. But I had good friends and people around me. I eventually rekindled that relationship with the woman I was in a situationship with and decided to embrace the feelings that I felt I couldn’t. I was in a relationship and I made her my gf. It felt good

About a month later my ex came back apologizing and saying how she missed me and wants to have a conversation about why she did what she did. There it was. All I ever wanted to hear for the past almost YEAR. And I couldn't. I was excited to see that and ashamed that I was excited. But I was also angry. Angry at her for waiting that long and angry for myself for having started moving on. Had to been a few months before I would’ve been able to hear her out. I told her I was in a relationship. She understood. It was the hardest thing l've ever done but I was proud (but pained) of my decision.

Me and my gf got closer over the next few months but her reaching out fucked my head up and made me feel even guiltier about the current relationship. I love her but I started feeling slowly that I got into this relationship partly from a sense of obligation and guilt. Especially given the fact that we were talking to each other around the same time. I feel shitty for that and broke things off because it was more authentic and fair to her than continuing knowing how I felt. It was never my intention to waste her time but those feelings I thought I was at peace with came back to the surface.

I know I made the right choice breaking up her. Not because I didn’t love her. But because I realized that I was lying to myself and her about how unbothered I was by my ex reaching out. How much I wanted to say yes. And how I feel that this relationship was built on a foundation of escapism (for both of us). There were also broader compatibility issues I overlooked but felt we could work through.

I grieved and tried to come to terms with that potential future being closed to me. Whether or not those feelings lingered I knew there was nothing there to hold onto and accepted that. But there was. And she was feeling what everyone told me she wasn’t. I hurt two women that I loved and lost both for the other. It’d be funny if it didn’t hurt so much.

Now I’m in a strange place. I want more than anything to reach out to my ex and finally have that conversation. But I know (like she must’ve) that time waits for no one. I’m sure it shattered her because it would’ve shattered me. Do I wait until I’m steadier and take a chance (the logical choice) or try to connect before she potentially finds someone new (the emotional choice). The irony is delicious but at this point it’s not a matter of IF but when. I want to wait for the “perfect” moment. I really do. When I have more money, when I have my own place. A better job. More time has passed since the breakup. But I’ve ran out of time so many times. Every day I don’t reach out is an exercise in self control but it feels like agony. Like I’m pretending I don’t care again…

I just want her to know. Deep down, after the heartbreak that I caused and that I went through, I know that I might not deserve what I want. But I see a future that’s worth every ounce of potential pain and I just want to be fully honest. She isn’t a rebound. This is what I’ve always wanted but tried to accept I couldn’t have. I love her and I can’t watch it slip away again without trying. It’s been months and she might’ve moved on or found someone else. All I can hope for is getting this off my chest and whatever happens happens. I just want to know if anyone else has been here? What do you think about my situation?

My father had a lot of health issues throughout the last 10 years. He was diagnosed with a blood dissorder initially but it was getting treated and he was ok. Then he was diagnosed with prostate cancer but overcame it and was ok. Then he had a pulmonary embolism and they found 20 blood clots in his lungs but he was ok. Then he had skin cancer 2 separate times and was ok after treatment.

About a year ago he started complaining about how a dental filling was irritating his tongue, and talked to his dentist about it but the dentist said it was normal. His tongue got worse and after 8 months his dentist agreed to send him for a biopsy. Biopsy confirmed oral cancer, and they were confident after surgery he'd pull through. He casually mentioned this to us over dinner and while we were taken aback, thought he'd pull through. He was 74. His surgery went great but they found a tiny bit of cancer in a node within his neck, so they recommended radiation to be safe. It was presented as a precautionary measure that would guarantee he'd beat the cancer.

After radiation every week day for 6 weeks, he had the worst side effects possible. He had severe third degree burns that disfigured his neck and face, lost teeth, was in extreme pain, couldn't eat solids and lost 40 pounds and almost had to go on a feeding tube, had zero energy, and got incredibly depressed. The doctors said this was all normal.

We started to notice weird things like him not getting better at all, falling asleep a lot while sitting up but then complaining he wasn't sleeping enough, socially withdrawing, and then he broke his ribs turning too suddenly. We just felt like something was up. He got a follow up CT scan that week, but on the next day, my mom was telling us he was acting really confused and delusional, so we took him to the ER.

ER confirmed high calcium in his blood, which caused the confusion. They suspected the cancer was back but didn't know where. His heart was also failing so they admitted him to oncology and had a cardiologist overseeing his care as well. His condition got from bad to worse and they were constantly putting out fires and couldn't get down to the bottom of what was happening, although they suspected cancer had metasticized. He started struggling to breathe and wasn't getting oxygen, so they had to send him to the ICU and started talking to us about life support and DNR protocols. We were in complete shock.

I'm the ICU we learned that there was lung aspiration, and he couldn't eat or drink without anything going to his lungs, and there was also tons of fluid in his lungs. He needed a feeding tube and tube in his lungs to constantly drain all of the fluid. He had pnemonia and they suspected cancer in the lungs caused it but couldn't confirm. Then they found out he had sepsis so they had to give him antibiotics through an IV, but his blood pressure was so low, they also needed to have him on pressers to get the antibiotics through. He wasn't getting enough oxygen so we had him on a CPAP - he had previously stated he didn't want to be intubated so we did CPAP. He needed a catheter as well. He had so many tubes in and out of him, and couldn't even talk. There were always tears running down his face, and he looked like he was in so much pain.

Because of his condition, he couldn't talk or eat for the last 6 months of his life. He was a wine snob and loved fine food, so to see him deprived of that and unable to join us for meals was horrible.

He was constantly delirious, but one day, seemed to be ok and more lucid. Everything was stabilizing, and the doctor said he thought he'd get through this, then we could transfer him back to oncology to figure out what was causing all of this. That night, things took a dark turn, and the ICU nurse called us all to come be with him. When I saw him, his eyes were bloodshot due to lack of oxygen, he looked so sad, and was unresponsive. They said his vitals kept dropping despite their extreme treatment, and the machines couldn't keep him alive anymore. He passed away at 4am that night.

I'm traumatized by how quickly and unexpectedly this all happened. None of us were prepared. We got his CT scan results after he passed, and they said there were some questionable spots on the other side of his neck, so they definitely figured it was cancer. If it was, he would have denied further treatment. All of his care team thought he'd pull through this, and it was a surprise to all of us.

My dad and I were never close it wasn’t a hostile or an abuse thing, we just somehow never clicked. He was sick for as long as I could remember, and doctors couldn’t pinpoint the cause, but they knew he had GERD. As I grew older, I became increasingly angry at him because he refused to take care of himself and defied all doctors’ orders to stop drinking, smoking weed, and cigarettes, saying that only that and fast food made him feel better. Considering what we now know about weed, I wouldn’t be surprised if it began as CHS and worsened since he had been smoking since he was a kid. 

When I turned 21, I decided to cut all contact with him and move on with my life. I still stayed friends with him on Facebook and would get updates about his hospitalizations. He would still claim not to understand what was happening, but he was convinced that doctors were lying, lazy, and not genuinely trying to diagnose his condition and just kept telling him to get sober. 

One day, I remember him reaching out to me on Facebook. He mentioned that he had spoken with one of the nurses who advised him to choose a next of kin to make medical decisions for him since his condition was getting worse and his hospital stays were getting longer(his decision to stay to try and make doctors find a diagnosis). Based on what he shared with me and others, doctors were still unable to identify any underlying issues and kept basing his symptoms on his lifestyle. I agreed and didn’t give it much thought, assuming he was just trying to guilt me into reaching out to him again. 

Two years ago, I got a call from his local sheriff asking if I had seen him. Neighbors had reported a welfare check on him, saying that they hadn’t seen him all day and the last time they saw him he was slurring and not making sense. They thought he was just drunk and maybe wandered off somewhere like he does sometimes. I decided to call my mom since they were still friends after the divorce and i didn’t know who he still talked to or where he lived, but she would know. She reached out to his friends, who informed her that they hadn’t spoken to him in a couple of weeks, saying he was starting to get weird and more aggressive so they were letting him cool off thinking he was just on a bender and would come back when he was done like he always did but, the last time they heard from him, he seemed his version of fine. 

Turns out he wasnt fine. Maintenance at his apartment was finally able to open his door 3 days later for “routine inspection” and found him alive but unconscious in his bed. They took him to the hospital and called me. 

Because he was unresponsive when they arrived, they did a full-body X-ray and found a mass in his frontal lobe. At that point, they couldn’t confirm yet whether it was an infection or a tumor, but it was the size of a tennis ball. They were leaning more to tumor based on x-rays but said they were waiting on the tech to fully confirm. Additionally, they discovered the early stages of aggressive lung cancer, which was not present when he had a chest X-ray six months before, they did at that time though, tell him that he would need to stop smoking because they were at the pint now where it had damaged his esophagus so badly that he would need surgery to repair it. He did not quit, but he was apparently in the process of thinking about quitting. 

They told me that they could treat him and maybe get him stabilized after being unconscious in a hot room for three days, but he would be coming back to fight terminal brain and lung cancer that would need intensive 24 hour care. I asked them to stop care, remove the ventilator and crank the pain killers and 3 days later he stopped breathing on his own and passed. 

His whole life, his greatest fear was that he had a fatal illness or cancer and would have to face it. So, when we were fighting to revive him from severe dehydration and a brain mass in the personality center of his brain, I made the decision not to let him live out his biggest fear. It seemed cruel to save him from dying so he could fight stage 4 lung and brain cancer and ultimately, no one in his circle who could financially and emotionally help him through it. 

The doctor praised me for my bravery in making this decision. He told me he regretted that he couldn’t make the same decision to end care when his mother was dying. Some of his friends thought I was a monster and petty for not doing everything I could to save him. His other friends, siblings, and my mother didn’t know that I had overheard them saying how relieved they were that it wasn’t them who had to make the decision because they couldn’t handle it. My grief group even joked that I had “won grief counseling” as the person with the most difficult story. 

I did experience grief for the first few months, but it was more about the loss of a relationship that we never had and never will have. But, for the past two years, the most difficult part has been struggling with the fact that I made a decision that ended in someone’s death. It feels like blood on my hands. Logically, I understand that this wasn’t what happened, and I know that he had a very slim chance of survival anyway and that due to the mass in his frontal lobe, we couldn’t have done anything to save him. But I don’t know that i will ever be able to stop thinking that way. 

Anyways tldr: dad was sick cuz he loves partying and made me end the party. He always said he was here for a good time not a long time. Dad please understand i made them CRANK those good drugs for you, but youre still our favorite asshole even if i couldn’t stand you.

I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have been with an amazing woman for six years. She wants to get married. I can’t explain why, but marriage sounds like the scariest thing on earth. She keeps telling me that nothing will really change in our relationship, and I believe that. But I just don’t see the point of getting married.

She brings up scenarios involving health, finances, and kids, but we could get many of those same protections through other forms of paperwork that don’t require marriage. After years of discussing it, she finally told me I had to make a decision: either we get married or she walks away. That was months ago. She’s already started packing.

I don’t want her to leave, but I also don’t want to get married. The worst part is that I can’t fully explain why. I’m a child of divorce. My parents had an abusive relationship, and I grew up around constant fighting: physical and verbal. Deep down, I know that’s where a lot of this comes from. After years of her encouraging me to go to therapy, I finally started a few months ago. But I still don’t have answers.Her parents have been married for over 30 years. I don’t know them very well, but they don’t seem particularly happy to me.Honestly, I don’t know anyone who’s married and happy.

She’s optimistic. She believes unhappy marriages happen because people choose not to work on them. Most of my friends who recently got married were together for nearly 10 years first. I always imagined something more like that. She points out that many of them started dating in high school, which is true, but I still feel like if a relationship can survive 10 years, marriage somehow feels safer.  
Everyone tells me I’m stupid. They tell me she’s a great person, a great partner, and that I’d be lucky to marry her.

They’re right.She is amazing.

But I feel like I’m not emotionally mature enough for her. I feel like I can’t give her what she needs. She’s articulate, self-aware, and really good at compromising. I’m afraid that if I propose just because she wants marriage, I’ll eventually resent her. I have a hard time letting things go.  
At the same time, she’s been trying to have this conversation for about two years. Looking back, my head was so far up my own ass that I couldn’t see she was trying to help me when she suggested therapy. I should have started two years ago.  
I can’t ask her to wait another two years.  
I don’t want to lose her, but I also don’t want to give her something half-assed.

Part of me hopes I can get my life together and come back for her later. Maybe we break up, she becomes free of all this stress, and I finally heal. Maybe she finds someone who’s ready for her. Maybe she doesn’t, and we reconnect someday.  
When I told her that, it made her very upset.  
She said she doesn’t need me to be healed. She already knows who I am. She said I can work on myself while staying in the relationship, that’s what she’s wanted all along.What she needs is marriage.  
She also told me there will be no future reconciliation if she walks out the door. If she leaves, she’s gone.

Part of me feels like I’m being strong-armed into a decision.My father says it’s my ego talking. It’s hard to take advice from him considering what he put my mother through.Sometimes I’m scared I’m just like him.He never realized what he had until it was gone. After all the abuse, he eventually fought for my mom, but by then she had moved on. I’d like to think he’s changed for the better, but he’s with a woman he doesn’t even seem to like. He doesn’t physically abuse her, but he’s a cheater, and he spends all day comparing his wife to my mother.  
I feel bad for her.

Clearly, I have a lot to work through.  
Part of me thinks I should just let my girlfriend go.  
But she told me something I’ll never forget:  
“The more I’ve learned about you, the more I’ve loved you. The more you’ve shared, the more you’ve run.” I think she’s right.  
I don’t think I like being seen.  
She knows me really well. She isn’t scared of me. She trusts me. I’ve never experienced anything like that before.

This is the kind of love I’ve always wanted.But I’m scared.And I’m afraid that fear is going to cost me the woman I love. I already know I’d regret losing her for the rest of my life.She has flaws, obviously, but she’s someone who actively works on herself. I’ve never seen anything like it.But I still don’t know what to do. I don’t feel like I can propose while feeling this conflicted. I’m scared I’ll resent her if I do. I’m also scared I’ll regret it forever if I don’t. I have too many negative feelings.Seriously, send help.

She’s already packing, but I feel like chasing after her right now isn’t a good look. It doesn’t feel romantic. It feels desperate.She deserves more than that.She’s leaving because she told me she isn’t willing to spend the rest of her 20s in a relationship like this.

For the most part, our relationship has been good. I just could never talk about the future without getting frustrated. We agreed on kids and other things. And I genuinely do want the other things. It’s just the concept of marriage. If you’re wondering why she stuck around this long because my friends and family have asked… I told her I’d do it. And I meant that I just was waiting for the right moment. I wanted to be sure. I’m sure about her I’m just not sure about marriage and she doesn’t get that. She sees it as the ultimate form of commitment but I’ve committed in other ways. We have a dog. We have a house. And I want us to have kids. I’m stuck.

At the end of July this year my best friend/cousin killed herself. While I knew how she felt about all the suffering she faced in life and knew she was in a lot of pain due to facing imminent kidney failure, her death still came as a huge shock to me.

In the weeks before she passed, I talked to her pretty much everyday (except for most weekends). I thought being a listening ear and just doing my best to support and make her feel seen was enough. I even stupidly thought I’d made a breakthrough 2 days before she passed, only to realize that’s probably the day she made her final decision. I realize now that I let myself be blinded by what I hoped would be, rather than what actually was. I know everyone dies, but I thought we’d be old in our rocking chairs laughing at how somehow we survived all the bullshit, at how we didn’t actually lose our minds even when life seemed like it would drive us crazy. I thought we’d have at least another 40-50 years to build the beautiful lives we wanted for ourselves, to support each other and grow old and prove to ourselves that just because life sucked as kids, we could and would somehow come out on top.

It’s been a lot to take in to say the least. On one hand, I feel guilty for even grieving because this is what she wanted, right? I feel like I’m selfish for not being able to accept and healthily cope with this. I feel like not moving on is somehow telling her that I don’t understand or get her, that I’m not loving her truly by being able to accept a choice she made that I never wanted. And it all just feels like I’m saying “why didn’t you do things my way, why didn’t you die on my terms, why can’t you stay around because you made my life brighter.” When in reality I know how much she was hurting, I don’t wish that pain on anyone. I don’t want her here and suffering, I just want her here living the life she truly deserves.

She left behind her fiancé and siblings, who are obviously devastated. I don’t know how to show up, especially because I don’t live nearby. I text, I call, I send songs that I hope might help listening to, I send memes that I hope will brighten their day, but it all just seems so pointless.

And in the midst of all this, I’m becoming angry and disappointed not just in life, but in the people I also had more expectations of. I’m particularly angry at her mom, who was abusive to her while she was here, yet feels the need to text me saying she hopes my friend knew how much she loved her (I had to listen to my friend 2 days before she died, cry to me, asking why her mother never loved her and never protected her), I’ve had to field the other family members who quite frankly I think are narcissistic enablers (though they mean well), telling me how to let bygones be bygones and forgive her mother.

I had to show up to her service, numb, while her mother pretty much made everything about her.

I’ve had to talk to the very people who while my best friend was alive told me how they thought she was negative and if she was going to kill herself and felt so badly, she should just do it. Even my own mother the day my friend died (though neither of us knew she had passed yet) said the same thing, when I told her that my friend didn’t need people telling her what to do with her health, she just needed support and people to care for her.

I’m so angry. And I’m angry at my job. I took 2 days off when I found the news (1 day to cope and then 1 day to fly for the service). I found out after I got paid that my approved PTO wasn’t being paid for because he found I was negative, even though my adp showed I still had plenty of PTO (still can’t get them to respond to any messages asking what my balance is and how to correct it in the system).

And my manager who said to let her know if I needed anything and that the company would support me, never even jumped in to say anything. IMO, even if I’m a few hours negative, there should be some bereavement policy. I wasn’t on vacation having a ball, I was processing her sudden death and attending her service.

On top of that, today I worked a half day and then let my manger know I wasn’t feeling well so would take the rest of the day off. All I got was a thumbs up response, no message saying to feel better soon, just a thumbs up. I just have a sixth sense that something changed the day I called and let her know about my friend passing. While my managers words tell me I’m doing a good job, her behavior doesn’t always seem to align with that and I’m feeling very hyper vigilant at my job, which is just adding to my exhaustion.

I know my productivity has been much lower lately, understandably so, yet I’m still completing my work and getting positive feedback from my project team members and the CEO. Ironically, I work for a mental healthcare corporation.

I’m just angry at how much people don’t actually seem to care or have any empathy and how they expect you to just act like business as usual. I find myself isolating now. I don’t want to attend family holidays, I don’t want to be around anyone, and it really feels like most people only care for you so much as you are productive and can do things for them.

Idk if anyone else has felt similar or has any words of encouragement/advice on how they healthily process grief. Thanks for listening, mostly just needed to vent and get this off my chest.

This Christmas will be the first one without my grandma. To me, she WAS Christmas: the warm hugs, the home-cooked Christmas foods, the well-thought through gifts, the one uniting the entire family, my best friend.

I want to tell you all about her life.

I genuinely believe she was the sweetest soul that has ever existed. She lived life with one rule: kindness. Never have I ever heard her speak badly about anyone. She thought good of pretty much everyone, and famously would listen to artists because “he/she/they seems so kind!” rather than the quality of the song or the artist’s voice.

Despite a very low pension/senior citizen pay: she’d make sure to EVERY MONTH donate to different charities. No matter how much pain she went through every single day due to the physical conditions she suffered the last 20 years of her life, she never complained. She would fight to be strong enough to meet family every week, with a smile on her lips.

Family was what was most important to her. She kept in contact with everyone (yes, that includes like 5:th cousins too) until the very end, making sure to regularly call those who live far away. She was very maternal and extra caring for the vulnerable: children, elderly, disabled and animals. She was very outspoken about their rights. For example, she often talked about how important it is to talk to an older person the same way you talk to anyone else - old people are not children - they have entire lifetimes of experience!

Throughout her entire career, she worked as a nurse at a mental hospital. Mental hospitals back then were a lot more inhumane than they are these days, and patients would go unnoticed and wrongly medicated. But my grandma always made sure to take well care of them despite the circumstances, to build personal bonds, and even invite her patients home to her place often. It made her so happy to know that she could help them somehow. She talked a lot about how some of her colleagues treated the patients very badly, which - for a moment - would fill her eyes with rage. She stood up to her colleagues several times, and never ever backed down when it came to her stance on this.

My grandma has always been a leading motivator for me academically. She has always stood there cheering me on, complimenting and letting me know how well I’ve been studying and how smart I am and how proud she is of me.

My sweet grandma always talked about how important it is to, as an older person, try to keep up with technology as much as possible. When I was a kid, she was the one who taught me how to use computers, how to print, and how to play video games! Some of my dearest memories are of my grandma and I playing Mario Kart together on her Nintendo.

She also taught me so many more things: how to knit and crochet (which are 2 of my biggest hobbies and creative outlets these days), how to bake gingerbread cookies, how to sew, how to do basic maths.

My family would always joke about how my grandma was a “chronic time-optimist”. Famously in my family, if there was a family dinner or event, it was important to tell my grandma that it started half an hour before it actually did - then she’d arrive same time as everyone else.

My grandma met my grandpa at age 17 at a bus stop when she was on her way to work. They later moved to the neighbouring city where they created a family, and, where I eventually grew up long after. Despite my grandma living in this city since being a young adult, she kept her accent from her birthplace - which she has always been very proud of.

When it comes to her birthplace, she was always excited to share her memories from it. Old stories about local celebrities, long-gone relatives, teachers that would treat students unfairly, and her childhood best friends - and she would always remember all of their names on the spot! She loved supporting the local ice hockey team, and small local bands.

The last month of my grandma’s life was hell. She had to be transported to the hospital by ambulance due to sepsis. At first she was critical and unconscious - then came the surge. It was like everything was normal again, and she was basically ready to leave the hospital. It was the biggest relief of my life. Then everything went bad again, and the experts said that she was likely not to wake up.

Then, like out of a miracle, she woke up once again! This time, however, she wasn’t her normal self. My grandma hasn’t been physically okay for a long time, but she’s always mentally been there (not shown a single sign of dementia). But when she had woken up, she had severe memory loss, she kept asking the same questions over and over again, confused, and - most of all - she would hallucinate.

First it was small things like “doesn’t that curtain look weird?”, “why is the wall moving a little bit?”, to full-on hallucinating people and events. One of the days, she said that I had come in earlier that day and “gave her ice cream”, another day she thought there was a dog in the room. Almost all of the days she saw her mum in a separate hospital bed in the corner of the room. She would keep pointing that way and ask the nurses if they had checked up on her mum’s well-being yet.

We would tell her when she was hallucinating and seeing things that weren’t real. She understood for the moment that she was seeing things that weren’t there, and could acknowledge it. At one point she stated “well, at least I’m hallucinating happy things - like my mother and a dog - rather than monsters and evilness!”. And, in a way, I’m happy her last moments were filled with happy hallucinations.

I love you forever grandma.❤️

When I lost my person, I had two days from the medical team telling me that there was no hope, to the day he was removed from life support and died.

During that two days, the organ donor representatives pulled me from his bedside to tell me he was an organ donor. I knew this, as I had been with him at the DMV when he was asked to check the box on his drivers license. His comment at the time was, "why not?" This is why not.

I had hope and believed that he would survive his illness, right up until it was outlined to me, by his medical team, that he could not. I was forced to accept that I would have to say goodbye to my heart. I asked for two days of life support, to give time for his friends and family to say goodbye, pray, come to terms, whatever. Part of me died making that decision.

On day one, of the last two, I made sure I styled my hair, and wore makeup. If he regained consciousness on one of those days, I wanted to be pretty for him. I wanted him to see the girl he was in love with, not the reduced hag-looking thing I had become. I wanted him to have some pleasure, and know that I would be ok. The organ brokers took that away.

I arrived at the hospital to regulations that full PPE was mandated. Gowns, gloves, and face masks. This was so that the organ donor business could assert to their buyers that anti-tuberculosis measures were in place. My love did not have, nor was he at risk for, tuberculosis. I fought this, because I did not want my heart and soul to be surrounded by masked, faceless attendants in his last two days. His doctors were pissed, because blood had been drawn (at the organ donors network request,) but tuberculosis testing had to be 'sent out' and would not have results for two weeks. He would be dead by then. I raged at the organ donor company. They asserted that the PPE measures had been put in place by the hospital, not them. When I informed the doctor, he literally ripped the directive off the wall, and told me that the "body brokers" always "pulled this shit." If the family objected, it overruled them. That was day one.

I went home and went to bed. At the time, I never slept, or ate, reliably. At 8:30 that night, I was deep asleep, when the phone rang. It was the organ donor company. Someone named Gretchen. She wanted to tell me that my husband had checked the "organ donor" box three times. She wanted to tell me that I had no say, and that my love's wishes would be honored. She told me that they would take whatever could be used (he died in complete organ failure, no usable organs) and there was nothing I could do about it. She straight told me I was a bad person for trying to usurp his wishes. She told me I would sit and wait for his body to be returned to his hospital room, and that was it. I was literally screaming. I was literally crying. She chuckled. She reiterated that I had no choice. I hung up.

She was right. Because my boy had checked that box (why not?) all rights were removed from his family. I'm not talking about a lifesaving liver or heart. He didn't have a single working organ. It's why he died. His blood, his bones, his muscle, his brain, all were fair game. These are not donated pieces. They sell them. It's a business. You donate, they sell for profit.

Her assertions were 100% correct. I had no choice, it was going to happen. There was nothing I, nor the hospital, could do to stop it. The doctors, and the nurses, were pissed that I had gotten that call. They called it "cruel" and "unnecessary."

I had no choice, but to accompany my love and my heart to a "pre surgical" suite where they would remove his life support. When he died, they would wheel him into surgery and dissect his body, and take the parts that were "donated" and could then sell. I went to that "pre surgical" suite, along with about 20 of his friends. I talked to him. I sang to him. I begged him to stay, once they removed life support. The body brokers only have two hours once life support is removed. If their "product" doesn't die in that time frame, the body is useless to them. He outlasted them.

He was taken back to his room in ICU. I thanked him. His nurses actually high-fived me, telling me that he must love me a lot, and there is no way he should have lived for two hours with no BP medication and no air. They called it a "last act of love, and a FUCK YOU to the body brokers."

He died shortly after being returned to his room. I played "Love and Mercy," and "Cowboy in the Jungle." The biggest, best, most charitable and giving part of me died that day.

I found out later, that even if you say "NO" on your driver's license, your family can make the decision to donate your organs. If you check "YES," all the decisions are taken out of your families hands. If the body brokers approach you to harvest bone, veins, skin, anything (it's all for sale,) if you checked "No," then your family can decide if it's appropriate. If you checked "yes" on your license, you've given consent for flesh peddlers to sell your remains.

Check "NO." If you've already checked "yes," change it and PUT IT IN WRITING SOMEWHERE THAT YOUR FAMILY HAS THE FINAL SAY. The organ donors network is not the lifesaving organization it was twenty years ago. It's a moneymaking grind.

My first encounter with debating was when I cut classes because my friend in a higher level invited me to watch a debate finals with their class. Long story short, it was heated in a way it's so refreshing to hear because both sides didn't back down and it was valid points back and forth, back and forth. It's not the kind of debate that rely on savage comebacks and call that 'witty', it's truly thought provoking and jaw dropping. And BOTH sides had people cheering loudly, I didn't know who was going to win.

So of course I was somewhat excited when we were assigned the same when we got to that grade. I'll admit I didn't do as good but it was different. That loud booming atmosphere? GONE. The room was dead silent for my match. It made me nervous but for my first time debating I thought it didn't matter, oh well. Until the next matchup came and suddenly my classmates had the capacity to cheer one side if not both after all. This wasn't a big deal but I was insecure about having no friends to cheer loudly even if the teachers demanded everyone to be quiet if it meant having your back, I don't get cheers unless it's already awarding. I felt lacking even if I pushed my best to guise myself as an extrovert. It's not that they didn't cheer because I sucked ass, oh I WON alr and everyone said it was deserved.

This is the case that made me hate debating officially. I got another debate assignment and I was kind of nervous given my last debate I cried for some reason lol (not the one I mentioned but not important). I'll admit I had a good group and everyone was looking at me like I'm going to save them from the depths of catching a low grade (I'm a transferee but I always get top notchers smthn like that). And preparations were smooth, we researched and planned carefully about counterarguments. Maybe this was finally the debate of a lifetime.

One thing we all didn't expect the next day, the main debater in the offensive was the class clown. I didn't think much of it because I studied all night digesting our hard-researched material but of course research is different from the actual thing.

Topic? Is bringing back extinct species a necessity? I say yes, they say no.

I did very well the first half given my group had to stop me from hogging all counterarguments that they prepared for and needed a grade. Not to be a pick me but I'm genuinely locked in and they kept saying "damnn did we really have that in those tiny index cards?". We already planned for me and another groupmate to take most of the heat once everyone got a turn.

Then in the second half they bring up one of their main arguments, that the reported chances of success were very low given the needed money so "humanity CAN'T pursue it". This was one of my expected problems but I prepared for it. My point was that (surprisingly) IVF have even lower success rates in 1900s, if they claim that humanity CAN'T pursue it then how have we been successful and bumped that 5% success rate in the present to a 79%? Not exact but that's the gist and we were citing specific research articles anyway.

Then their counterargument to that? "OP name but in a savage tone, what does pregnancy have to do with reviving dead animals?". I assumed he didn't understand my counter but before I can explain the ENTIRE classroom went "ohhhh shiiii" "GOTTEM" and laughed at my previous counter. I explained it again but then his counter was "Okay but ANIMALS are different from BABIES? Amirite? pan to the crowd" And the audience fucking hollered again. That's the entire comeback, to all the numbers I mentioned and stayed up late for THAT'S what they consider valid?

The rest of the match we countered other points and the other side kept dismissing ours and moving on. After the encounter I froze in my seat and stared at the floor the rest of the closing speeches. I won best debater and our team won but there's still a hole in my chest. I don't consider myself having an ego but I guess it worsened my inferiority complex.

I cried to sleep that day. Not because I was going to lose but genuinely felt like a fucking fool. I hated them for that. I pulled an all nighter to help my friends but in the midst of it I felt played. I thought it was going to go away since we got ANOTHER short debate and still, I wasn't able to bring up my points well because their tactic was to keep interrupting even.

I cried AGAIN, in class but I didn't sniffle, I let my eyes well up with tears. Everyone was so loud when it came to me talking but everyone respectfully piped down when it's one of our well respected and revered classmates. This was about respect now, everyone and I mean EVERYONE didn't want me to talk and shut up. Everyone cared more for the hypothetical grade (IT WASN'T GRADED EVEN) than letting me continue. They didn't interrupt me with an argument, they all SHUSHED me as in "shhh shh shhh counterargument".

I handled some accidental dismissals from my old school so I'm used to that since we all get caught up in the moment, but not this level of rudeness. It's different when 5 of your friends are rooting for the opposing side but still cheering for you too when you have a turn, from your entire classroom close to 50 students all tell you to shush. It's honestly worse that they're not barbaric cuz I'd expect it, I just didn't expect my classmates who are so kind to each other shut me down like that. I thought I would finally get over my self confidence issues but it made it worse.

I just want that kind of respect I have for them. I guess respect is not earned but bandwagoned by whoever was here first.

Even though she is cancer free, she’s still dealt with a lot of physical issues in the aftermath and I’ve been her biggest confidante.

I’m only 27, and I’ve lost these incredibly meaningful relationships. I fear people have become desensitized to the phrase “depression”

They hear it and assume it’s a phase that will pass. It’s not until someone has lived it, felt it, breathed it that they can understand the weight, understand the hate, that you feel for yourself, for everything, for everyone, only then can they relate. You suffocate: The stuff that you carry, the stuff you try and bury, underneath layers of fake, and telling everyone that you’re okay. 

Your arms heavy, heart unsteady, your knees feel frail like if you take one step they will buckle underneath you, crumbling you to the bottom of the earth. You pray that one day you will muster the courage to disappear.

You deflate, degrade, berate yourself until you used up all the words out of the dictionary. You claw and gnaw at the fragile lines that cover your skin because nothing will change you nothing will make you feel okay but at least this way the pain isn’t just in your heart. 

You tell yourself you deserve it as the alcohol burns your throat to the point where words become shallow. Your heart, hollow; drowning in sorrow. Gasping for air that isn’t there, you’re sinking, drowning and you don’t even care. 

It feels like an anchor is tied to your ankle, pulling you down with the weight it takes.

Every mistake. Everything you do no matter the intention will be the undoing of you. While others live their lives you try and try to keep them afloat by breaking off pieces of you. But one wrong move, one wrong piece and they’ll turn their backs, taking your peace. You have to be nice all the time because any less than nice is a version of you they wish to not see wish you not to be.

They tell you to reach out when it’s swallowing you whole. When you have no hope. So you do. You tell every possible soul. You trust that your friends will be there to help you through this storm. But once again, you experience nothing but disappointment and you’re left out worn. They abandon you when you’re at your lowest. But weren’t you always the ones who brought them gifts, said the compliments, gave the advice you could only wish someone would give to you? You handed them parts of you but that’s what’s funny. Double standards: because when it’s their turn to care, they suddenly have no pieces to spare, not even the ones you gave them to wear. Because once the pieces are used to fix others, they no longer fit back in your puzzle.

They watch you, they see your mood change. They see your dark days. They know about your pain, because you told them. You told them you needed to be saved. But saved isn’t what they know how to do. They only know how to take and take until there’s nothing left of you left to break. They see your mistakes. The way you’re not fully there, the way you snap easily without a care. But now you’re falling apart, the simplest things irritate. Patience runs thin, you start to hate. They watch and turn away like it’s not their place. It’s not their job to analyze you; like fixing you means carrying too much weight. They see how far your feelings dragged you down, why would they risk it? Why would they drown? So they give you space, leaving you to be left without a trace. 

You’re alone. You’re always alone. They make plans without you and then suddenly you become the reason their plans are unknown.

“You haven’t been wanting to hang out lately”   
“You’re always locked in your room being lazy”  
“You’re so angry all the time, you’ve been acting crazy”  
Did you even ask me? Did you try to get through? Did you show me the same care I once showed for you? Did you bring me my favorite candy or ask to play my favorite game? From my favorite restaurants, are there any leftovers with my name? But no, don’t worry, I’m the one to blame. You all hang out, no “wish you were here” but it’s my fault when I want to disappear?

 Friendship is a one way street. Say “depressed” and you’re suddenly too much to keep. You’ll be fine, they think. You’ve always been fine. But they don’t see your hazy days, the empty gaze, staring at nothing, your mind in a craze. They don’t see what you do to just be okay. They don’t see how many days, you went through alone just so you’d stay. How many times can you break, how much more can you take? Before there’s nothing left of you to remake.

Everyone these days has depression. It’s the way of life. So they brush over it, no empathy to be spared, no stories to be shared because they’ve healed from theirs. They hear you say you’re suicidal, but they think you’re being dramatic. The signs weren’t there. Of course they’re not, not when I hid them behind a mask so to not make you worry. But then I tell you my story. All the roads I’ve paved. The attention I so desperately chased. Not because I seek to be seen but because I craved to be saved. How could I want to die when I barely even lived? Living a life that I struggled to give, the love, the care, the joy it needed to forgive. 

So no depression is not just a phrase, not just a phase. It follows you like a shadow, turning your mind into a maze. You want to be okay. You’re tired. You’ve hit your limit. You called out for help. What more can you do for yourself? What more can you do when you can’t even save yourself from you?
